vignette:
Rajesh's Vigil

Rajesh Patel had returned from Syria eighteen months ago with a commendation letter and a wound he could not name. At thirty-five, he was a tax consultant in Chicago, a position that seemed, in the abstract planning of his recovery, perfectly suited to rebuilding a normal life-contained, predictable, numerical. His wife Priya had been relieved when he took the job. But the spreadsheets that once calmed him now became battlegrounds for his attention. Numbers would blur mid-calculation. He would find himself staring at a column of figures for ten minutes without registering a single entry, his mind elsewhere, reconstructing sequences of events that refused to arrange themselves in any coherent order.

The field hospital in Aleppo had been a converted school. Rajesh had been there as a medic with an international relief organization, one of four staff members managing a rotating schedule across three rooms. On the morning of March 14th, the building had been struck. He remembered the sound first-not the explosion itself, but the silence that followed it, a silence so complete it seemed to have weight. He remembered running toward the rubble, his body moving through doorways and past collapsed walls, stepping over things he would not allow himself to fully see. He remembered the smell, acrid and chemical, mixed with something else-burning flesh, burning fabric, burning everything-a smell that had entered his nostrils so completely that for weeks afterward he could taste it. He had found two colleagues in the second room, both dead. He had not been able to protect them. He had not even been in that room. The randomness of that fact-that he had stepped out moments before, that he had survived by accident-had corroded something foundational in how he understood the world. If survival was arbitrary, if protection was impossible, then what was the point of anything?

Now, when smoke drifted from a neighbor's barbecue, Rajesh's body seized. His hands would rise to his face, pressing hard against his eyes and nose as if he could unsee and unsmell the past. Priya had stopped inviting friends over. She had stopped suggesting they go anywhere, really. Last month, his mother had died-peacefully, at home, of natural causes-and the funeral had been unbearable. The cemetery itself was a trigger; the gathering of grief-stricken people was a trigger; even the gentle expressions of sympathy from relatives had felt like accusations. When his uncle had simply placed a hand on his shoulder, Rajesh had flinched so violently that he had knocked over a flower arrangement.

At work, his performance was declining. He had missed two client meetings because the thought of sitting in a conference room while someone-a colleague, a client-raised their voice in even mild frustration sent him into a state of hypervigilance that made concentration impossible. Any expression of anger, even a calmly stated disagreement, felt like an imminent threat. His manager had begun to notice. There had been a difficult conversation last week about his reliability.

The nights were the worst. Rajesh could not sleep past 3 a.m., and when he did sleep, his body would jolt awake at the smallest sound-the house settling, a car passing on the street, Priya shifting beside him. He felt safer during daylight, though safety was perhaps the wrong word. Daylight was merely less dangerous. He had come to believe that the world was fundamentally chaotic, that people he cared about could be taken away without warning or reason, and that he was fundamentally alone in this knowledge. Priya tried to reach him, but he could not let her. To let her close felt like inviting her into the line of fire.

What had finally brought him to therapy was a moment of clarity that had terrified him more than the memories themselves. He had been sitting at his desk, unable to work, unable to think, and he had realized that he was avoiding everything that might make him feel better-he had turned down an invitation to his closest friend's engagement party, he had stopped the evening walks he used to take with Priya, he had even stopped calling his sister. He was, he understood with sudden certainty, disappearing. And the shame of that-the shame of having survived when others had not, the shame of being unable to protect anyone, the shame of being broken-was becoming too heavy to carry alone.
